light.notes: At least 6 hours of sun: a sunny windowsill, or outdoors in warm weather.

water.notes: Keep lightly moist, watering at the base in the morning. Small pots can need water daily in summer.
water.restingSeason: Basil is an annual that dies in the cold. Indoors in winter, give it your brightest spot and less water.

guides.feeding: Liquid feed every 2 weeks when you're harvesting heavily.
guides.pruning: Pinch out the tips just above a pair of leaves, and nip off flower buds, to keep it leafy.
guides.propagation: Seed, or cuttings rooted in water within a week.

problems.fix: Keep it somewhere warm, away from cold windows at night.

problems.cause: Dozens of seedlings crammed into one small pot
problems.fix: Tease it into 3–4 clumps and pot each separately in fresh compost.
Pinch out flowers early and harvest from the top regularly.

guides.growthHabit: Bushy annual herb with soft, aromatic leaves.

water.notes: Likes moist soil. Water pots often and garden plants in dry spells.
water.growingSeason: Keep pots moist; they dry out fast.
water.restingSeason: Dies back in winter; keep just damp.

soil.notes: Moist, fertile soil. Grow it in a container — its roots spread aggressively through beds.

toxicity.notes: The ASPCA lists garden mint as toxic to cats and dogs; eating large amounts can cause vomiting and diarrhoea.

guides.feeding: Liquid feed monthly for pots in summer.
guides.repotting: Divide and repot every year or two; old clumps die out in the middle.
guides.pruning: Harvest regularly and cut to the ground in autumn.
guides.propagation: Division, or cuttings rooted in water.

problems.fix: Cut the plant back hard and bin (don't compost) the affected growth.
Grow it in a pot, or a bottomless container sunk in the ground.
Divide it and replant young pieces from the edge.

guides.growthHabit: Spreading perennial herb with running roots.

water.notes: Keep the soil moist.
water.restingSeason: Dies back in winter; keep just damp.

soil.notes: Moist, fertile soil, ideally in a container to stop it spreading.

toxicity.notes: The ASPCA lists mint as toxic to cats and dogs; eating large amounts can cause vomiting and diarrhoea.

guides.feeding: Liquid feed monthly for pots in summer.
guides.pruning: Harvest often; cut to the ground in autumn.
guides.propagation: Division or cuttings — it rarely comes true from seed.

problems.fix: Cut back hard and bin affected growth.
Contain it in a pot.

guides.growthHabit: Spreading perennial herb with purple-tinged stems.

light.notes: Full sun. Indoors it struggles without a very sunny window.

water.notes: Drought-tolerant once established. In pots, water when the top few centimetres are dry — it dies from both waterlogging and drying out completely.
water.restingSeason: Sparingly.

soil.notes: Free-draining, gritty soil; it's fine in poor soil.

guides.feeding: Rarely needed; a little in spring for pots.
guides.pruning: Trim after flowering. Don't cut into old, bare wood, which rarely regrows.
guides.propagation: Softwood cuttings in spring or summer.

problems.cause: Powdery mildew from still, humid air
problems.fix: Give it more sun and airflow.

problems.cause: Root rot from wet soil — or a pot left bone dry
problems.fix: Improve drainage and water when the top few centimetres are dry.
Trim lightly every year after flowering.

guides.growthHabit: Evergreen, woody shrub with needle-like aromatic leaves.

water.notes: Let the soil dry out between waterings.
water.restingSeason: Very little; winter wet is its main enemy.

guides.repotting: Replace plants every 3–4 years as they get woody.
guides.pruning: Trim lightly after flowering to keep it compact.

problems.fix: Trim after flowering, and replace old plants.
Add grit and raise pots onto feet.

water.notes: Keep the soil moist; it bolts when dry.
water.restingSeason: Less, keeping it just moist.

toxicity.notes: The ASPCA lists parsley as toxic to cats and dogs in large amounts: it can make skin sensitive to sunlight.

guides.pruning: Harvest the outer stems first, at the base.
guides.propagation: Seed, which is slow to germinate — soak it overnight first.

problems.cause: It's a biennial in its second year, or stressed by heat or drought
problems.fix: Sow fresh seed each year and keep it watered.
Water regularly and thin seedlings.

guides.growthHabit: Clump of curly or flat divided leaves; flowers and dies in its second year.

water.notes: Keep moderately moist.
water.growingSeason: Water in dry spells; pots often.
water.restingSeason: Dies back in winter; keep just damp.

toxicity.notes: The ASPCA lists chives as toxic to cats and dogs. Like onions and garlic they can damage red blood cells and cause anaemia; cats are especially sensitive, and signs can take days to appear.

guides.feeding: Liquid feed after each heavy cut.
guides.pruning: Cut to 5cm above the soil; it regrows several times a year. The flowers are edible too.

problems.cause: Low light or an overcrowded clump
problems.fix: Divide it and give it more sun.
Cut down and dispose of affected leaves.

guides.growthHabit: Clump of hollow, grass-like leaves with purple pompom flowers.

light.notes: Sun in spring and autumn; light shade in summer slows bolting.

water.notes: Keep lightly moist. Drought makes it run to seed.
water.restingSeason: Less in cool weather.

guides.propagation: Sow seed where it will grow — it resents being transplanted — every 3–4 weeks for a steady supply.

problems.fix: Sow directly in cooler weather, keep it watered and give it shade in summer.

guides.growthHabit: Fast annual herb with lacy leaves.

water.notes: Water young plants until established; after that it rarely needs it. Pots need water in dry spells.
water.restingSeason: None; keep it out of winter wet.

soil.notes: Poor, free-draining, even chalky soil. Rich, wet soil kills it.

toxicity.notes: Listed as toxic to cats and dogs. Eating it can cause nausea and vomiting, mainly from linalool.

guides.pruning: Trim after flowering, staying just above the woody base — cutting into old bare wood kills that part.

problems.fix: Prune every summer; replace very old plants.
Replant in gritty, free-draining soil.

guides.growthHabit: Compact, evergreen shrub with grey leaves and scented flower spikes.

light.notes: Sun or part shade, sheltered from cold winds.

water.notes: Water pots when the top few centimetres are dry.
water.restingSeason: Sparingly.

toxicity.notes: Listed as toxic to cats and dogs; eating it can cause vomiting and diarrhoea.

guides.feeding: Balanced feed monthly for pots in spring and summer.

problems.fix: Check drainage and feed in the growing season.
Pick off affected leaves and wipe off scale.
Move pots to shelter; trim damage in spring.

guides.growthHabit: Evergreen shrub or tree with aromatic leaves; often clipped into shapes.
guides.matureSize: 1–2m in pots; much larger in the ground

light.notes: 6–8 hours of sun, outdoors or in a greenhouse.

water.notes: Water deeply and consistently. Irregular watering causes split fruit and blossom end rot.
water.growingSeason: Daily for pots in hot weather.
water.restingSeason: It's an annual and dies with the first frost.

soil.notes: Rich compost; in pots, at least 10 litres.

toxicity.notes: The ASPCA lists the tomato plant as toxic to cats and dogs: the leaves and green stems contain solanine. Ripe fruit is fine for people; don't eat the foliage.

guides.feeding: High-potash tomato feed weekly once the first fruits set.
guides.pruning: On tall (cordon) varieties, pinch out the side shoots that grow between stem and leaf. Bush varieties don't need it.
guides.propagation: Seed sown indoors in early spring.

problems.symptom: Black, sunken patch at the bottom of fruit
problems.cause: Blossom end rot, from irregular watering
problems.fix: Water deeply and consistently.

problems.symptom: Brown blotches and collapsing leaves in wet weather
problems.fix: Remove affected growth immediately; grow under cover or choose blight-resistant varieties.
Keep it watered and sheltered.

light.notes: Full sun for the sweetest fruit.

water.notes: Keep moist, especially while fruiting. Water at the base, not over the fruit.
water.restingSeason: Very little while dormant.

guides.feeding: High-potash feed every 2 weeks from flowering.
guides.pruning: Remove runners unless you want new plants; clear old leaves after fruiting.
guides.propagation: Peg down runners into small pots.

problems.fix: Put straw under the fruit and remove affected berries promptly.

problems.symptom: Fruit eaten before you get it
problems.fix: Net the plants and use slug protection.
Replace with young plants from runners.

guides.growthHabit: Low, clump-forming perennial that spreads by runners.

light.notes: As much sun as possible: outdoors in summer, your brightest window in winter.

water.notes: Water thoroughly when the top few centimetres are dry, then let it drain.
water.growingSeason: Often weekly or more in pots.
water.restingSeason: Less, but don't let it dry out completely.

toxicity.notes: Listed as toxic to cats and dogs. Oils and psoralens in the leaves and peel can cause vomiting, diarrhoea and skin sensitivity to light.

guides.feeding: Summer citrus feed weekly from spring to autumn; winter citrus feed through winter.
guides.propagation: Grafted plants fruit far sooner than seedlings.

problems.fix: Check the drainage and use a citrus feed.

problems.cause: A sudden move indoors into dim, warm air
problems.fix: Keep it in the brightest, coolest room (10–15°C) and water less.
Wipe them off with a damp cloth.

guides.growthHabit: Evergreen shrub or small tree with fragrant flowers and fruit.

light.notes: Full sun. Indoors, only the sunniest windows will do.

water.notes: Drought-tolerant. Water pots thoroughly when the top half of the compost is dry.
water.growingSeason: Weekly for pots in hot weather.
water.restingSeason: Sparingly.

guides.feeding: Balanced feed monthly for pots in spring and summer.
guides.pruning: Thin and shape in late spring.

problems.fix: Move it outside or into the sunniest spot.

problems.cause: Sooty mould growing on sticky scale insect honeydew
problems.fix: Deal with the scale; the mould washes off.

guides.growthHabit: Evergreen tree with silvery, narrow leaves and a gnarled trunk with age.

water.notes: Keep moist.
water.restingSeason: Dies back; keep just damp.

soil.notes: Moist, fertile soil — contained in a pot.

toxicity.notes: The ASPCA lists mint as toxic to cats and dogs; large amounts cause vomiting and diarrhoea.

problems.fix: Cut back and bin affected growth.
Grow in a container.

water.notes: Keep lightly moist, watering in the morning.
water.restingSeason: Most are annuals that die in the cold.

problems.fix: Keep above 10°C.
Pinch out flowers.

water.notes: Let the soil dry between waterings.
water.restingSeason: Very little.

problems.fix: Trim after flowering; replace old plants.
More grit.

water.notes: Drought-tolerant once established.
water.restingSeason: None.

toxicity.notes: Lavenders contain linalool; eating them can cause nausea and vomiting in pets. French and Spanish lavenders are also less frost-hardy than English lavender.

problems.fix: Trim yearly after flowering.
Sharper drainage; shelter tender types.

water.notes: Water thoroughly when the top few centimetres are dry.
water.restingSeason: Less, never bone dry.

toxicity.notes: Citrus leaves and peel contain oils and psoralens that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea and light-sensitive skin in pets.

problems.cause: Low light and warm dry air
problems.fix: A bright, cool room.
Wipe off.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Evergreen shrubs and trees with scented flowers.

water.notes: Water in dry spells; ornamental bulbs need little once the foliage fades.
water.restingSeason: Keep bulbs on the dry side.

toxicity.notes: Onions, garlic, leeks, chives and ornamental alliums can all damage red blood cells in cats and dogs, causing anaemia. Cats are especially sensitive, and signs can take days to appear.

problems.fix: Plant in free-draining soil.
Remove affected leaves.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Bulbous plants with grassy or strap leaves and ball-shaped flower heads.
